119.title: The Bestowals of Christ Michael
119.b0.ask: “Why did the Creator who made the universe have to come down and live seven times in the likeness of his own creatures?”
119.b2.p: In Paper 118 we saw the Supreme and the Ultimate in relation to time and space, and how creature experience takes part in the evolution of Deity. Paper 119 shows how this principle was actually worked out in the Creator Son of our own local universe. The paper is presented by Gavalia, Chief of the Evening Stars of Nebadon.
119.b3.p: A Creator Son organizes and governs his universe, but he takes a solemn oath to the Trinity not to assume full sovereignty until his seven creature bestowals are completed and certified by the Ancients of Days. These Sons are innately just and naturally merciful, but through their bestowal experiences they become understandingly merciful in new ways. Michael of Nebadon made his bestowals about one hundred and fifty million years apart, and the last of them took place on Urantia.
119.b4.p: In whose likeness, then, did Michael come down, one after another? And what did those seven experiences leave in him and in his universe?
119.b5.q: ⟦Q 119:8.2⟧Michael was born a creator, educated an administrator, trained an executive, but he was required to earn his sovereignty by experience.⟦/Q⟧
119.b8.p: Almost one billion years ago, Michael placed Nebadon in the care of his elder brother Immanuel. Saying only that he went “⟦Q 119:1.1⟧to do the bidding of my Paradise Father,⟦/Q⟧” he vanished from Salvington. On the third day a strange Melchizedek Son, accompanied by a solitary omniaphim, appeared on the receiving field of the Melchizedek world.
119.b9.p: For one hundred years he served on twenty-four missions of universe emergency, and by his matchless wisdom and supreme love he became chief of Melchizedeks. The records do not state that he was Michael, but it is universally believed that he was. How such a bestowal is accomplished remains a secret of Sonarington.
119.b11.p: About one hundred and fifty million years later, Lutentia, the System Sovereign of system 11 in constellation 37, led a rebellion. Three days after Michael again took leave, a new and unknown Lanonandek Son was assigned to that system as acting System Sovereign.
119.b12.p: For more than seventeen years he set the troubled system in order with justice and mercy, even offering his rebellious predecessor a share of the throne. Lutentia spurned the offer, but millions of his followers accepted the forgiveness of the new ruler, who became known as the Savior Sovereign of the system of Palonia. On the day he left, even Lutentia confessed: “⟦Q 119:2.6⟧Just and righteous are you in all your ways.⟦/Q⟧”
119.b14.p: The third bestowal took place on planet 217 in system 87 of constellation 61, in a system where another System Sovereign had gone astray. Michael appeared as a strange Material Son and was made acting Planetary Prince. Working alone for one whole generation on a world cut off from the outside universe, he brought about the repentance of the defaulting Planetary Prince and his staff and restored the planet to loyalty.
119.b15.p: All three bestowals were equally mysterious. Each time he appeared suddenly, as a fully developed member of the bestowal group.
119.b16.t: One hundred years; twenty-four emergency missions
More than seventeen years of universe time
One whole generation of planetary time
119.b17.p: Since this bestowal, no Material Son or Daughter in Nebadon has complained of their assignments, for they know their sovereign has in “⟦Q 119:3.7⟧all points been tried and tested,⟦/Q⟧” as they are. And none has ever knowingly joined in rebellion against Michael.
119.b19.p: Fourth, Michael appeared as an unknown seraphim of the supreme order. For more than forty standard years he served as a seraphic teaching counselor to twenty-six master teachers on twenty-two worlds. During that age all supreme seraphim were treated with special care, lest anyone should find he had unawares been host to the Sovereign of the universe.
119.b20.p: Michael had now experienced the life of three orders of his created Sons and of the angels, and next he turned to the ascending career of his lowest will creatures, the evolutionary mortals. As the bestowals went down to lower forms of life, Gabriel became more and more involved as the liaison between Michael and Immanuel.
119.b22.p: A little over three hundred million years ago, Michael announced that he was going to Uversa and departed. But the one who arrived there was an unnumbered ascendant pilgrim of mortal origin, known on Uversa as Eventod. For eleven years he lived as a spirit mortal, tested and tried like his fellows.
119.b23.p: This first appearance of Michael in the role of a stage of mortal evolution thrilled all Nebadon, and the Melchizedek colleges began to teach that he might someday incarnate as a mortal of the flesh. Yet even Gabriel confesses that he does not comprehend how it is done.
119.b25.p: This time, for the first time, Michael revealed the rest of his plan. He would live as a morontia mortal at the headquarters of the fifth constellation, and his seventh and final bestowal would be made on some evolutionary world in the likeness of mortal flesh. His career on Endantum was one of the most extraordinary epochs of all his bestowals, but the author is forbidden to reveal its details.
119.b26.p: When Michael returned, it was plain to everyone that the Creator had become a fellow creature. To the millions who welcomed him back, he gave only this reply:
119.b27.q: “⟦Q 119:6.5⟧I have simply been about my Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧”
119.b29.p: The announcement that Michael had chosen Urantia for his final bestowal was made shortly after the default of Adam and Eve became known. The universe expected him to come again as a grown individual, but he was born in Bethlehem as a helpless infant. It was the most precarious step in all his career.
119.b30.p: Joshua ben Joseph, the Jewish baby, was conceived and born just as all other babies, and he was reared in the ordinary manner by parents who were average people of their day. The only supernatural event connected with his birth was the announcement by the seraphim to a group of Chaldean priests led by Ardnon. How the Creator becomes incarnate in the likeness of his creatures will forever remain the secret of Sonarington.
119.b32.p: After his bestowal on Urantia, Michael was proclaimed the settled ruler of Nebadon. The eighth proclamation came from Uversa, and a joint pronouncement came from the Father and the Son. When the Trinity Sons were about to withdraw, Michael personally asked them to remain forever on duty in Nebadon. It took almost one billion years to complete his bestowal career and establish his supreme authority.
119.b33.p: Each bestowal revealed one of the wills of the Deities, personalized in the Seven Master Spirits. None of the bestowals revealed God the Supreme by itself, but the sum of all seven is a new Nebadon revelation of the Supreme Being.
119.b34.t: The will of Deity he lived
The united will of the Father, Son, and Spirit
The will of the Father and the Son
The will of the Father and the Spirit
The will of the Son and the Spirit
The will of the Conjoint Actor
The will of the Eternal Son
The will of the Universal Father, as a mortal of flesh and blood
119.b35.p: So Urantia became the sentimental shrine of Nebadon and the mortal home of Christ Michael — a Melchizedek minister, a system savior, an Adamic redeemer, a seraphic fellow, and a Son of Man. And Jesus has promised sometime to return to this World of the Cross.
119.b36.q: ⟦Q 119:8.8⟧Urantia is the sentimental shrine of all Nebadon, the chief of ten million inhabited worlds⟦/Q⟧
119.b38.p: Paper 119 is the story of a Creator who did not rule by power alone. He earned his sovereignty by personally living the lives of his creatures, from a Melchizedek all the way down to a mortal infant. With each bestowal he went a little lower, and the universe loved and trusted him all the more. A rebel system accepting forgiveness, Material Sons who ceased to complain, angels who came to honor one another — all were fruits of that experience. And because his final step was taken on our world, little Urantia became the place that all Nebadon holds in its heart.
119.b39.t: The ruler of the universe served for a hundred years as an unknown Melchizedek
A Savior Sovereign restored a rebel system with justice and mercy
An emergency Material Son reclaimed an isolated world
As a seraphic teaching counselor he lived the life of the angels
He lived on Uversa as Eventod, an unnumbered ascending pilgrim
As a morontia mortal, the Creator became a fellow creature
He was born on Urantia as a helpless infant
The seven bestowals won his sovereignty and newly revealed the Supreme
119.b41.box: By living the lives of his creatures himself, the Creator becomes an understanding and merciful sovereign.
120.title: The Bestowal of Michael on Urantia
120.b0.ask: “Why did the Creator Son lay aside all his power and choose to come into this world as a helpless baby?”
120.b2.p: In Paper 119 we saw how Michael became sovereign of Nebadon through seven bestowals. Paper 120 returns to the moment just before the last of them, the bestowal on Urantia, began. It is presented by the Melchizedek director of the revelatory commission.
120.b3.p: At any moment Michael could have ruled his universe in his own right as a Creator Son. But he did not wish to rule merely in his own isolated right. He desired to rule with the wisdom of the Supreme Being, gained through actual experience in co-operative subordination to the Paradise Trinity. That is why his power is unlimited, his authority is unquestioned, and his sovereignty is supreme. Just before he left, he placed all authority in the hands of his elder brother Immanuel, who then gave him his prebestowal counsel.
120.b4.p: What, then, did Immanuel ask of the Creator who was going to live as a man? And who was Jesus, both God and man?
120.b5.q: ⟦Q 120:4.4⟧Never lose sight of the fact that the supreme spiritual purpose of the Michael bestowal was to enhance the revelation of God.⟦/Q⟧
120.b8.p: Immanuel first points out how this bestowal differs from the others. Until now Michael had always appeared as a fully developed being, but this time he would go to a disordered planet as a helpless babe and pay the full price of bestowal. In his earlier bestowals he had been subject to every phase of the divine will except the personal will of the Father; in the seventh he would be wholly subject to the Father’s will.
120.b9.p: Michael had voluntarily laid aside all extraplanetary support. Just as his creatures depend on him, he would now be wholly dependent on his Paradise Father. In this way he would come to know the full meaning of the faith-trust he had always asked of his creatures.
120.b10.q: “⟦Q 120:1.4⟧Throughout your Urantia bestowal you need be concerned with but one thing, the unbroken communion between you and your Paradise Father⟦/Q⟧”
120.b11.p: Immanuel then guarantees the safety of the universe. By mandate of the Ancients of Days nothing of serious import could happen in Nebadon during the bestowal, and any new rebellion would carry within itself the seed of its own annihilation. All the delegated authority remained Michael’s, and he could take it back at any moment he chose.
120.b13.p: Immanuel gives nine charges in turn. At their heart is the request that Michael achieve his work as the Son of Man, in weakness made powerful by faith-submission to the will of his Father. Having refused to crush the rebels by his creator prerogatives, it was fitting that he should now, in the likeness of his lowest creatures, wrest dominion from their hands.
120.b14.t: Charge
What it asks
1. Preparing the bestowal
Grow up as a child, live by the Father’s will, and ascend to receive sovereignty
2. Ending the Lucifer rebellion
Technically terminate the rebellion in Satania as the Son of Man
3. The title of Planetary Prince
Atone for the confusion left by Caligastia and the Adamic default
4. Dispensational judgment
Resurrect the sleeping survivors and open the age of the Spirit of Truth
5. The role of teacher
First free man’s spirit, then heal minds, then minister to physical well-being
6. Spiritual freedom
Pour out the Spirit of Truth and open the way to the Adjusters
7. A life for the whole universe
Not an example for one generation, but an inspiration for all worlds
8. The great mission
Reveal the Father to man and man to God
9. A warning about creator attributes
Refrain from forming any superhuman will to power
120.b15.p: The fifth through seventh charges set the direction of this life. He was to be a teacher who would first free and inspire man’s spiritual nature, illuminate darkened minds, and release them from age-old fears — and only then attend to physical comfort. In his life the will of the finite creature and the will of the infinite Creator were to become one. His life was not to be an example for the people of his day or for later generations to copy, but an inspiration for all lives on all the worlds of Nebadon in every age.
120.b16.p: The eighth charge shows the heart of the bestowal: within one short life in the flesh, to show both God seeking man and finding him, and man seeking God and finding him. The ninth reminds him that, though he would in fact be an ordinary human, he would remain in potential a Creator Son, and so he should refrain from any superhuman will to achievement.
120.b18.p: Immanuel then adds eight further advices, arrived at in consultation with Gabriel. They explain many features we see in the earth life of Jesus. One of them is that his life and teachings should become not the property of one sect but the common heritage of all religions and all peoples.
120.b19.t: Also show things immediately helpful to his fellow men
Follow the accepted family customs of his time
Avoid economic and political entanglements; work for spiritual regeneration
Do not interfere with the normal evolution of the races
Leave no writings, and let no images of himself be made
Leave no human offspring on the planet
Leave them to the Adjuster, the spirit, and the judgment of his human mind
120.b20.p: These advices kept the life of Jesus from being confined to any narrow mold. He was to avoid entanglements with politics and economics and not interfere with the normal evolution of the races, yet he was free to leave behind an improved system of positive religious ethics. The advice to leave no writings or images was given so that nothing potentially idolatrous would remain. All other details were left to the indwelling Adjuster, the divine spirit, and his growing human mind. The result might not look perfect to any one man in any one generation, but it would be wholly and supremely complete as judged on the perfected worlds.
120.b21.p: When he had finished, Immanuel declared that he now reigned as acting sovereign of Nebadon, and he committed the Son of Man about to be to the keeping of Gabriel. Then, in the presence of all Salvington, Michael vanished from their midst.
120.b23.p: Those who had accused Michael of selfishly seeking power were to be silenced forever by the life of self-forgetful service that the Son of God now entered upon as the Son of Man.
120.b24.p: The paper stresses that Christ Michael, while truly a dual-origin being, was not a double personality. He was not God in association with man but God incarnate in man. He did not progressively become God, nor did God at some moment become man; Jesus was God and man — always. The only thing that grew was his human mind’s realization of this fact.
120.b25.t: Dual in origin, yet one personality
Not God in association with man, but God incarnate in man
Not gradually become, but always God and man
The human mind’s recognition of this fact
120.b26.p: Even to citizens of the local universe, the most intriguing of miracles is the incarnation of a Paradise Son. Yet through all this extraordinary experience, God the Father chose to manifest himself as he always does — in the normal, natural, and dependable way of divine acting.
120.b28.p: Before telling the story of Jesus’ birth, Paper 120 first explains why his life had to take the shape it did. Michael laid aside all support not because he lacked power, but because he wanted the experience of depending wholly on the Father’s will. Immanuel’s counsel set the direction of that life: to be a teacher who frees man’s spirit first, to leave behind no sect and no idol, and to live not for one generation but for the whole universe. And the Jesus who was born in this way was not half God and half man, but one person who was God and man from beginning to end.
120.b29.t: The first bestowal without any support, depending on the Father alone
Achieve it not by power but in weakness made strong by faith
A heritage for all, leaving no sect, no writings, no images
Jesus was always one person, God and man
120.b31.box: The Creator laid aside his power and lived as a man, wholly dependent on the Father’s will, and by that life he revealed God to man and man to God.
121.title: The Times of Michael’s Bestowal
121.b0.ask: “Why did the Creator Son choose that very age, and that very land, in which to be born as a man?”
121.b2.p: In Paper 120 we watched Michael lay aside all his powers and set out for Urantia. Now Paper 121 takes a wide look at the stage on which he would be born: the world of the first century. From this paper on, the life of Jesus is told by a secondary midwayer who was once attached to the apostle Andrew.
121.b3.p: The narrator tells us that Andrew refused to let copies of his own record be multiplied. He knew how careful the Master had been to leave no written record behind him, and a similar attitude among the other apostles greatly delayed the writing of the Gospels.
121.b4.p: What kind of world, then, was Jesus born into? And how did the politics, philosophy, and religion of that age both prepare the way for a new gospel and stand in its way?
121.b5.q: ⟦Q 121:1.1⟧When Michael incarnated on Urantia, the world presented the most favorable condition for the Creator Son's bestowal that had ever previously prevailed or has since obtained.⟦/Q⟧
121.b7.h: 1. The Occident of the First Century after Christ
121.b8.p: Jesus did not come in an age of spiritual decadence. He came at a time when spiritual thinking and religious living were reviving. Greek culture and the Greek language had spread far and wide. The Jews, part Occidental and part Oriental in nature, were well fitted to carry a new religion both east and west, and the tolerant rule of Rome made this easier still. Paul — a Hebrew of the Hebrews, a Roman citizen, who preached in Greek — shows how all of these came together in one man.
121.b9.t: Influences that bound European civilization together
Language and culture, and some philosophy
The rapid spread of religious and moral teaching
121.b10.p: The Mediterranean world was one empire. Good roads linked its centers, and pirates had been swept from the seas. Yet under this outward peace and prosperity most people lived in poverty, and a happy middle class hardly existed yet.
121.b12.p: Palestine was the crossroads where three continents met. Most of the caravan routes from the East passed through it on their way to the Mediterranean ports, and more than half of that traffic went right by the little town of Nazareth. Over two hundred synagogues scattered across the Roman world became the cultural centers where the new gospel would first be received.
121.b13.t: What they prepared for the new gospel
121.b14.p: Even under Roman overlordship, the Jews enjoyed a good deal of self-rule and waited for the Messiah, a great deliverer. The paper explains that they credited the independence they had gained by political luck to their being a “chosen people.” This made Roman rule all the harder to bear, and it kept them from learning that their mission was spiritual, not political. In those days Galilee was more gentile than Jewish.
121.b16.p: Roman society was made up of five well-defined strata. The paper explains that half the population of Rome were slaves; the ablest of them could buy their freedom and rise to high places, and the early church was made up largely of the lower classes and the slaves.
121.b17.t: The ruling group, with money and official power
Merchant princes, bankers, and traders across the empire
Few in number, yet the moral backbone of the early church
Free men, but competing with slave labor
Half the population; some bought their freedom and rose
121.b18.p: Most people did not think their class unjust. So the paper says plainly:
121.b19.q: ⟦Q 121:3.9⟧Christianity was in no sense an economic movement having for its purpose the amelioration of the miseries of the depressed classes.⟦/Q⟧
121.b20.p: Women had more freedom in the Roman Empire than in Palestine, but the Jews far surpassed the gentiles in their devotion to family life.
121.b22.p: In the minds of the nobler gentiles there was a soil of goodness in which the seed of Christianity could take root. The gentile world of that day was ruled by four philosophies, all growing out of Platonism.
121.b23.t: The pursuit of happiness; it fought fatalism and superstition
A controlling Reason-Fate; virtue is its own reward
Man can save himself; simplicity and virtue
Certainty is impossible — a negative outlook
121.b24.p: Stoicism rose to a sublime morality that no purely human philosophy has ever surpassed. Yet it never became a religion, because its followers failed to see themselves as the children of a loving Father. The Cynics drew much from what remained of the teachings of Machiventa Melchizedek, and they prepared the common people for the later missionaries. But on the whole these philosophies belonged to the strong and the wise. They were not a religion of salvation for the poor and the weak.
121.b26.p: The religions of earlier ages had been mainly tribal or national affairs. They did little to satisfy the personal longings of the ordinary man. In the Occident of Jesus’ day there were four kinds of religion.
121.b27.t: Greek and Latin mythology joined with patriotism and tradition
Men deified and worshiped; it led to persecution
A Babylonian pseudoscience turned into a religion
New cults from the Levant that promised personal salvation
121.b28.p: The mystery religions shared a myth about a god who died and returned to life, a brotherhood that crossed racial lines, elaborate ceremonies of initiation, and a promise of survival after death. The paper warns us not to confuse Jesus’ teaching with them. Still, by revealing a hunger for personal religion, these cults helped prepare the way for Jesus.
121.b29.t: Moral redemption and a new life
From sin, and toward righteous character
The historic fact of Michael’s bestowal
121.b30.p: To such a generation, perplexed by incomplete philosophies and complex cults, Jesus gave his gospel of personal religion.
121.b31.q: ⟦Q 121:5.18⟧To this same generation he subsequently gave his gospel of personal religion—sonship with God.⟦/Q⟧
121.b33.p: Religious thought in Jerusalem in Jesus’ time had been strongly influenced by Greek culture and philosophy. Three languages were spoken in Palestine, and the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures was the decisive influence that later sent Paul’s Christianity flowing west instead of east.
121.b34.t: The educated classes and the better strata of Jews
121.b35.p: Philo of Alexandria was a great teacher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Hebrew theology. The paper names him as one of seven human teachers who combined the better elements of earlier teachings: Sethard, Moses, Zoroaster, Lao-tse, Buddha, Philo, and Paul. Philo had left behind the doctrine that sin can be forgiven only by the shedding of blood. Paul’s doctrine of original sin, by contrast, came partly from Mithraism and had little in common with what Jesus taught.
121.b36.p: The scattered Jews all looked to the temple at Jerusalem, and as many as two and a half million of them came to the city for the great feasts. Eastern and Western Jews were of one mind in making Jerusalem the center of their worship and in looking for the Messiah.
121.b38.p: The paper explains that the Jews of that day had built a solid wall between themselves and the gentile world. They had fallen into a self-righteousness that leaned on the letter of the law and on false pride of descent. That is why they found it so hard to accept Jesus’ teaching of the spiritual brotherhood of all men. What bound them was a bondage far more real than Rome’s — the bondage of ritual and tradition.
121.b39.p: Jeremiah had spoken of a law written in men’s hearts, and Ezekiel of a new spirit living in man’s soul. But when Jewish religion became trapped in the inertia of tradition, the stream of religious evolution passed westward to the peoples of Europe. In Paul’s Antioch cult, the gospel of Jesus was mixed with other teachings.
121.b40.t: What was blended into Paul’s Christianity
Redemption and atonement through the sacrifice of a god (Mithraism)
121.b41.p: The people of that time believed that spirits dwelt even in rocks and trees, and everyone took miracles as commonplace. Small wonder they were astonished at the new proclamations of the carpenter of Nazareth.
121.b43.p: The midwayer narrator had the help of the lost record of the apostle Andrew and of celestial beings, yet he chose to use the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as well. The paper explains how the four Gospels came to be written.
121.b44.t: John Mark, from Peter’s memories; finished in A.D. 68
Isador, a disciple of Matthew; Pella, A.D. 71
The son of David, the fulfillment of prophecy
Luke the physician, from Paul’s story; A.D. 82
The friend of publicans and sinners
Written by Nathan in A.D. 101, at John’s urging
The ministry in Judea and around Jerusalem
121.b45.p: These writers portrayed Jesus honestly, as they had seen, remembered, and learned. Their records are imperfect, yet they were enough to change the course of Urantia history for almost two thousand years. The narrator explains that wherever possible he used human records and human concepts first, and turned to superhuman sources only when these fell short.
121.b46.q: ⟦Q 121:8.14⟧In many ways I have served more as a collector and editor than as an original narrator.⟦/Q⟧
121.b48.p: Paper 121 shows that the life of Jesus did not begin in a vacuum. Rome’s roads and peace, Greece’s language and philosophy, and the synagogues of the scattered Jews had paved the road on which the new gospel would run. People looked for morality in philosophy and for a promise of salvation in the mystery cults, yet they never reached a personal religion in which they were children of a loving Father. Jesus came when that hunger was deepest. And the midwayer who tells his story humbly admits that his account gathers and weaves together the thoughts of many human minds — and so he opens the door to the life story that follows.
121.b49.t: The Occident of the First Century after Christ
Roman, Greek, and Jewish influences made it the most favorable time
A crossroads of three continents and scattered synagogues became the road for the gospel
A society of five classes; Christianity was no economic movement
The four philosophies served the strong, not the salvation of the weak
The hunger shown by the mystery cults prepared the way for personal religion
The Greek scriptures and Philo sent the gospel flowing west
The bondage of tradition passed religious evolution on to Europe
The four Gospels, imperfect as they are, were enough to change history
121.b51.box: The Creator Son came when the hunger for personal religion was deepest and the roads were best prepared, and he gave the gospel of sonship with God.
122.title: Birth and Infancy of Jesus
122.b0.ask: “Why was the Creator of a universe born in the home of an ordinary carpenter, just like every other baby?”
122.b2.p: In Paper 121 we surveyed the wide world of the first century into which Jesus would be born. Now Paper 122 narrows its gaze from that broad stage to a single family, and to the birth of a single child.
122.b3.p: The paper admits that it will hardly be possible to explain fully why Michael chose Palestine, and why he chose the family of Joseph and Mary. Michael decided on Urantia in counsel with Gabriel, and Gabriel judged the Hebrews to be the bestowal race. A commission of twelve then studied Jewish home life and recommended three couples. From these, Gabriel himself chose Joseph and Mary.
122.b4.p: Who, then, were these two people? How did the child of promise come into the world? And how far apart were the hopes of men and what really happened?
122.b5.q: ⟦Q 122:8.2⟧In just the same manner as all babies before that day and since have come into the world, the promised child was born⟦/Q⟧
122.b8.p: Joseph was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, though he carried a mixture of several non-Jewish strains, and he was not a direct descendant of David or Solomon. His ancestors were craftsmen — builders, carpenters, masons, and smiths — and Joseph himself was a carpenter. Mary was a woman of ordinary temperament, but she came of a line that included many remarkable women of history. The paper explains that she was a Jew by culture and belief, but by inheritance she carried a wider mixture of strains than Joseph did.
122.b9.p: Of all the couples considered, Joseph and Mary combined most ideally a broad heritage with personal qualities above the average. Michael wished to come as an ordinary man, so that common people could understand him and receive him. That is why Gabriel chose just such people as his parents.
122.b11.p: Jesus’ life work really began with John the Baptist. Late in June of 8 B.C., Gabriel appeared to the childless Elizabeth and announced the birth of her son John, who would be the forerunner of the divine teacher. Her husband Zacharias doubted for a long time. Only her pregnancy and a dream of his own at last convinced him.
122.b12.p: In November of 8 B.C. Gabriel also appeared to Mary, and Mary went to visit Elizabeth, a distant cousin, staying with her for three weeks and growing firm in her faith. John was born on March 25, 7 B.C., and from childhood his parents taught him that he was to grow up as a spiritual leader.
122.b14.p: One evening about sundown, Gabriel appeared to Mary beside a low stone table. He told her that she would bear a son, whom she was to call Joshua, and that he would inaugurate the kingdom of heaven on earth and among men.
122.b15.q: ⟦Q 122:3.1⟧This home has been chosen as the mortal habitat of the child of destiny.⟦/Q⟧
122.b16.p: Joseph trusted Mary deeply, yet for many nights he could not sleep. How could the child of human parents be a child of divine destiny? The paper explains that Gabriel’s visit took place the day after Jesus was conceived, and that it was the only supernatural event in the whole story of his conception and birth.
122.b18.p: Joseph came to believe only after a vivid dream. In it a messenger told him that the child would come first to his own people, who would hardly receive him, but that to all who did receive him he would reveal that they were the children of God.
122.b19.p: The paper stresses that none of these visits made any mention of the house of David, a deliverer of the Jews, or the Messiah. Jesus’ mission was not for one group but for all races and peoples. Here is how later interpretations compare with what the paper explains:
122.b20.t: A descendant of the royal house of David
Joseph belonged to the “⟦Q 122:4.2|122:4.3|122:4.4⟧house of David⟦/Q⟧” only by adoption
Most of these prophecies were made to apply to him afterward
The original read, “⟦Q 122:4.4⟧a maiden shall bear a son⟦/Q⟧”
The genealogies of Joseph and Mary
Constructed after his earth life; not to be depended upon as factual
122.b22.p: Joseph and Mary were opposites in temperament, and Jesus inherited a harmonious blend of both. On the whole, though, it was Mary’s hopeful and determined nature that shaped the course of his life.
122.b23.t: Gentleness and sympathy for human nature
The gift of a teacher and righteous indignation
Ritual training and knowledge of the Hebrew scriptures
A broader outlook and spiritual freedom
122.b24.p: Both were well educated for their time, and both were good teachers. Their courtship began on the day Mary brought Joseph a cup of water. They married when Joseph was twenty-one and built a new home in Nazareth. Most of Joseph’s family later believed in Jesus, but very few of Mary’s relatives ever did.
122.b26.p: Jesus’ home stood on the edge of Nazareth, near the highest hill in southern Galilee. Because of this he could often walk in the countryside and climb to the top of the hill.
122.b27.p: The house was a one-room stone building with a flat roof, and an adjoining building for the animals. Its furniture was a low stone table, some dishes, a loom, a lampstand, a few stools, and mats for sleeping. The young Jesus used to feed grain into the mill while his mother turned it. As the family grew, Joseph added another room, which served as a carpenter shop by day and a bedroom at night.
122.b29.p: The census ordered by Caesar Augustus was carried out a year late in Herod’s Palestine. Mary did not have to go, but she insisted on coming along. She was afraid she might give birth alone while Joseph was away, and she also wanted to see Elizabeth.
122.b30.t: They leave Nazareth at dawn and spend the first night by the Jordan
They pass the foot of Mount Sartaba and lodge at an inn in Jericho
They visit the temple in Jerusalem and reach Bethlehem in the afternoon
122.b31.p: On the way they talked about the child’s future: Joseph pictured a spiritual teacher, Mary a deliverer of the Hebrew nation. In Bethlehem every room was taken. They settled in a granary at the front of a caravan stable cut out of the rock, and counted even this good fortune.
122.b33.p: At noon on August 21, 7 B.C., with the help of women who were fellow travelers, Mary gave birth to a son, and the baby was laid in a nearby manger. On the eighth day he was circumcised and named Joshua. Seraphim sang over the manger, but human ears did not hear them. No one came to worship the baby except the priests from Ur.
122.b34.p: The paper also explains how the story of the star of Bethlehem arose. That year there were three unusual conjunctions of Jupiter and Saturn, and well-meaning enthusiasts of a later time built a beautiful legend around this natural event.
122.b35.t: A star guided the wise men
The wise men saw no star
The wise men worshiped the child
Three priests from Ur came, guided by Zacharias
A visit on the night of his birth
The visit came almost three weeks after his birth
No one came before the priests
122.b37.p: Following the law of Moses, Joseph and Mary went to the temple in Jerusalem to redeem Jesus as their firstborn son and to offer the sacrifice for Mary’s purification. Simeon, a singer, and Anna, a poetess, had learned the secret from Zacharias. By a sign agreed on beforehand they recognized the child, and Simeon sang a hymn that Anna had composed.
122.b38.p: The hymn sang of a light to lighten even the gentiles. Yet on the way home Joseph felt uneasy about these attempts to hurry Jesus into the role of the Jewish Messiah.
122.b40.p: When Herod heard reports of the visit of the priests from Ur and of the song in the temple, he sent men out to find the child. Joseph was poor, yet he was afraid even to go out looking for work. After more than a year without finding the child, Herod ordered that the boy babies of Bethlehem under two years of age be killed, and sixteen babies lost their lives in a single day.
122.b41.p: But there were believers in the Messiah even at Herod’s court. One of them told Zacharias of the order, and Joseph’s family fled to Alexandria in Egypt the night before the slaughter. They stayed there two full years and returned only after Herod had died.
122.b43.p: Paper 122 clears away the many legends that grew up around Jesus’ birth and shows us the simple facts. Gabriel’s announcement was the only supernatural event. The child was born like every other baby and laid in a manger in the granary of a stable. He was raised by a thoughtful carpenter father and a cheerful, practical mother in a one-room stone house. The people around him hoped he would be a deliverer seated on David’s throne, but the message heaven sent spoke only of the kingdom of heaven and of being children of God. By entering an ordinary life, the Creator made it possible for anyone to understand him.
122.b44.t: An ordinary couple, yet ideal, with a broad heritage
The birth of John the forerunner was promised first
The only supernatural event in the whole story of his birth
The Messianic prophecies and Davidic descent were added later
He inherited the natures of a thoughtful father and a cheerful mother
He grew up simply, in a one-room stone house
On the census journey they lodged in a granary beside a stable
He was born like every other baby; the star legend came later
The song of Simeon and Anna revealed the hope for a Messiah
They fled to Alexandria to escape the slaughter of the infants
122.b46.box: The Creator was born without miracles, an ordinary baby in an ordinary home, so that anyone could understand him and receive him.
123.title: The Early Childhood of Jesus
123.b0.ask: “How did the Son of God grow up as an ordinary boy — asking, learning, and playing?”
123.b2.p: In Paper 122 we saw Jesus born in Bethlehem and carried off to Alexandria to escape Herod. Now Paper 123 follows his early childhood, from his infancy in Alexandria to about his eighth year in Nazareth.
123.b3.p: In Alexandria Joseph worked as a foreman of laborers and began to dream of becoming a builder. Mary was the most devoted of mothers, yet she came to see that overprotection could make a child self-centered, and so she let Jesus grow up like other children. The believers of Memphis and Alexandria gave the family a copy of the Greek scriptures and urged them to stay in Egypt, but in 4 B.C. they returned to Palestine. Mary wanted to live in Bethlehem; Joseph chose Galilee for the child’s safety and education.
123.b4.p: What kind of home and school, then, did the boy Jesus grow up in at Nazareth? And what questions did he ask along the way?
123.b5.q: ⟦Q 123:5.8⟧Jesus was highly educated in that he thoroughly understood men and devotedly loved them.⟦/Q⟧
123.b8.p: The family quietly returned to Nazareth and, for the first time since Jesus’ birth, settled in a home of their own. Jesus was three years and two months old. He missed his friends in Alexandria, yet he was delighted to have a home of his own. Joseph and Mary agreed not to tell the people of Galilee that Jesus was a child of promise, and they faithfully kept that agreement.
123.b9.p: In his fourth year Jesus became a lifelong friend of Jacob, a neighbor boy, and his brother James was born. Joseph built a workshop near the village spring, beside the caravan resting place, and Jesus grew up there hearing the stories of caravan travelers from every corner of the earth.
123.b11.p: On February 11, 2 B.C., Jesus reached the age of his first wholehearted moral decision, and a Thought Adjuster came to dwell with him. This Adjuster had served before with Machiventa Melchizedek. Like countless other children, Jesus did not know that the divine Monitor had come. From this day his guardianship was entrusted to the Adjuster and to the seraphic guardians.
123.b12.p: His sister Miriam was born. From five to ten years of age Jesus was one continuous question mark. The most valuable thing in his early training was that his parents answered his questions honestly and with care. The Galilean Jews divided a child’s life into seven stages and taught their children systematically.
123.b13.t: From the first to the eighth day
To the end of the fifth year
Sons are given over to their fathers to be taught
123.b14.p: On August 21, 2 B.C., Mary formally handed Jesus over to Joseph for his instruction. Still, his mother went on teaching him to garden, and had him practice writing Aramaic, Greek, and Hebrew in a sandbox on the roof of the house.
123.b15.h: 3. Events of the Sixth Year (1 B.C.)
123.b16.p: Joseph taught Jesus Greek from the copy of the Greek scriptures given them in Alexandria. Since there were only two such copies in all Nazareth, seekers after truth were always coming to the house. Before he was six, Jesus asked his father what caused an earthquake, and Joseph answered, “⟦Q 123:3.2⟧I really do not know.⟦/Q⟧” It was the first great shock of his life. Very early, too, Jesus began to doubt explanations that blamed natural happenings on invisible spirits.
123.b17.p: After a visit from the family of his cousin John, Jesus became interested in the history and feasts of Israel, and Joseph explained the meaning of each one.
123.b18.t: The temple dedication of Judas Maccabee; eight days of candles
The deliverance of Israel through Esther
The week of unleavened bread and the pilgrimage to Jerusalem
The most solemn feast of the new year
A national vacation, camping out in booths
123.b19.p: That year Jesus’ prayers puzzled his parents a little. After saying the prayers he had been taught, he always insisted on having “⟦Q 123:3.6⟧just a little talk with my Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Joseph widened his work as a builder, and his income tripled. Jesus went with his father to neighboring towns and watched how people lived. Joseph patiently explained the reasons behind the family’s discipline, and then Jesus gladly cooperated.
123.b21.p: In January of this year Nazareth had its heaviest snowfall in a hundred years. Children of that time played much at weddings and funerals, but there were few organized games. Jesus had a gift for humor and play, but little chance to show it; even so, he was cheerful on the whole until he was fourteen. Mary sold pigeons, and Jesus managed the charity fund made up from what she earned.
123.b22.p: During an unusual sandstorm in July, Jesus fell down the stone stairs. The paper explains that this was no neglect on the part of midwayers or seraphim; it was an accident that could not have been avoided. Celestial personalities do not arbitrarily step into ordinary physical events. Even in special cases, midway creatures may intervene only at the command of their superiors.
123.b23.q: ⟦Q 123:4.7⟧Material accidents, commonplace occurrences of a physical nature, are not arbitrarily interfered with by celestial personalities.⟦/Q⟧
123.b25.p: At seven Jesus entered the synagogue school. He already spoke Aramaic and Greek well, and now he learned Hebrew. The pupils had no textbooks; they learned by repeating together, in unison, the sentences spoken by their teacher, the chazan.
123.b26.t: The basics of the Hebrew law
Memorizing the deeper teachings of the law
Returned to the parents as a “⟦Q 123:5.2|124:5.4⟧son of the commandment⟦/Q⟧”
123.b27.p: The paper explains that Jesus was educated in three places. Nazareth was a caravan crossroads with many gentiles, and a place where the traditional law was interpreted freely. Jesus spoke Greek with caravan travelers of many peoples. The chazan said he seemed to learn more from Jesus’ questions than he had ever taught him.
123.b28.t: Equipment of mind and heart for grappling with the problems of life
123.b29.p: The “birthday text” Jesus chose was a passage from Isaiah: to preach good tidings to the meek, and to proclaim liberty to the captives. On Sabbath afternoons he climbed the high hill with his father, looked out over Mount Carmel and Mount Hermon, the Jordan valley and the Mediterranean, and listened to the story of Elijah. Before he was eight he talked with the village mothers at the spring, and he learned to milk, to make cheese, and to weave.
123.b31.p: Jesus was not a brilliant pupil, but he was diligent, and he stood in the upper third of his class. Each month he spent a week with an uncle who was a fisherman or one who was a farmer. He learned mathematics from a teacher from Damascus, and he traded dairy products for harp lessons, so that by eleven he was a skillful harpist. Nor did he ever stop asking awkward questions — about the dry and rainy seasons, or why the heat and cold changed as they did.
123.b32.p: That year Nahor, a rabbi teacher from Jerusalem, came and urged that Jesus be educated in Jerusalem. Mary half agreed; Joseph hesitated. The decision was left to Jesus. Two days later, after talking with his Father in heaven, he answered that he would stay at home.
123.b33.q: ⟦Q 123:6.9⟧They who love me so much should be able to do more for me and guide me more safely than strangers who can only view my body and observe my mind but can hardly truly know me.⟦/Q⟧
123.b35.p: The young Jesus of Paper 123 is no wonder-working prodigy. He is a boy who asks endless questions, who falls, plays, and learns. He was surprised that his father did not know everything, he asked the meaning of every feast, and he insisted on talking with his heavenly Father as with a friend. His true education came from the love of his home, the teaching of the synagogue, and his dealings with all kinds of people at the spring and in the workshop. A Thought Adjuster quietly came to dwell in his mind, and the boy chose to grow up beside the parents who loved him. In this way the Son of God skipped not a single step of ordinary human growth.
123.b36.t: Keeping the secret of the child of promise, they settled into an ordinary home
The Thought Adjuster came, and the age of endless questions began
Events of the Sixth Year (1 B.C.)
The first shock — even his father did not know — and his talks with his heavenly Father
Celestial beings do not arbitrarily interfere in unavoidable accidents
He learned about men at home, in the synagogue, and among people
He chose his loving parents over schooling in Jerusalem
123.b38.box: The Son of God grew up as an ordinary boy, asking and learning, and he skipped not a single step along the way of growth.
124.title: The Later Childhood of Jesus
124.b0.ask: “Caught between his own convictions and obedience to his parents, how did the boy Jesus come to understand his mission?”
124.b2.p: In Paper 123 we watched the boy Jesus in Nazareth grow to the age of eight, asking and learning without end. Now Paper 124 follows him from nine to thirteen, up to his first Passover pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
124.b3.p: The paper says that had Jesus stayed in Alexandria, he might have enjoyed better schooling, but that schooling would have followed purely Jewish lines. In Nazareth he grew up in surroundings where he had to work out the problems of life for himself, and he met all kinds of people from every part of the civilized world. He was better prepared to understand the gentiles, and he gained a more balanced view of the Eastern and Western schools of Hebrew theology.
124.b4.p: What, then, did Jesus run up against in these years, and what did he accept? And when did he first become aware of his mission?
124.b5.q: “⟦Q 124:6.15⟧The hour has come. It is time that you began to be about your Father's business.⟦/Q⟧”
124.b8.p: In the winter of his ninth year, Jesus challenged his teacher over the teaching that all images and pictures were idolatrous. It came out that he had drawn a charcoal picture of his teacher on the schoolroom floor, and the elders came to see Joseph. Jesus stated his views without fear, yet declared that he would abide by his father’s decision. Joseph chose to uphold the rabbis’ interpretation, and giving up a favorite pastime became a great trial for the boy.
124.b9.p: That year Jesus climbed to the top of Mount Tabor for the first time, and at a workbench Joseph had built for him he made a yoke with his own tools. Seeing ice for the first time, he thought long about how water can exist as a solid, a liquid, and a vapor. The paper adds that the personality within this boy was in fact the creator of all these things.
124.b10.p: Before he was thirteen he had learned a little of nearly every trade practiced in Nazareth, except metalworking. His parents began to learn from him, and before he was ten he had become the leader of a band of seven boys who had gathered of their own accord.
124.b12.p: On the Sabbath of July 5, A.D. 4, walking in the country with his father, Jesus first voiced thoughts that showed he was becoming aware of the unusual nature of his mission. Joseph and Mary listened closely, but they gave him no information.
124.b13.p: His playmates saw nothing supernatural in him. The most unusual thing about him was that, even when wronged or insulted, he would not fight for his own rights. His neighbor and friend Jacob, a year older, always stood up for him. He was a beloved leader whose sympathy came close to wise compassion, and he enjoyed talking with grown-ups about culture, politics, and religion.
124.b14.t: His first trip to look over the fisheries on the Sea of Galilee
His close tie to his father’s trade
A new kind of religious teacher
His final choice, shaped by many influences
124.b16.p: Joseph and Mary were tempted to treat Jesus as special, but they wisely held back, and Jesus himself was quick to refuse special favors. This was his last year of carefree play. When his brother Jude was born, his mother fell seriously ill, and from just before his eleventh birthday he took on the responsibilities of the eldest son.
124.b17.p: On a trip with his father to the Greek city of Scythopolis, Jesus admired the clean streets, the amphitheater, and the athletic games, and he suggested that Nazareth build an amphitheater too. It was the only time Joseph ever lost his temper with him. Jesus answered, “⟦Q 124:3.8⟧Very well, my father,⟦/Q⟧” and never raised the subject again as long as his father lived.
124.b18.p: Even so, all his life he sought to make room for wholesome recreation, both in his own living and later in the plans for the work of the twelve apostles. From this year he entered a period of deep meditation, and he began to think that his work must not stop at uplifting the Jewish people alone.
124.b20.p: Jesus now worked regularly in the carpenter shop and was allowed to manage his own earnings. He also learned the wisdom of not showing anything that would make him seem different from others. The paper explains that, because he was a single personality, it was actually hard for him to become aware of the dual origin of the natures that made up that personality.
124.b21.p: Joseph and Mary sensed more and more that there was something superhuman in their son, yet they lived and died without knowing that he was the creator of a universe. Jesus leaned increasingly toward his father’s spiritual views, and his mother was hurt that her son did not fulfill her hopes. When his parents explained why images were forbidden, Jesus pointed out that kissing the parchment on the doorpost was idolatry for the very same reason — and Joseph took the parchment down.
124.b22.p: His greatest conflict in these years lay between two commands. He never shirked the duty of reconciling them, and in the end he blended them into a masterful concept of group solidarity based upon loyalty, fairness, tolerance, and love.
124.b23.t: “⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Be loyal to the dictates of your highest convictions of truth and righteousness.⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Honor your father and mother, for they have given you life and the nurture thereof.⟦/Q⟧”
124.b25.p: At thirteen Jesus passed from boyhood to young manhood, and his youngest brother, Amos, was born. In the middle of February he became humanly assured that he was destined to perform a mission on earth for the enlightenment of man and the revelation of God. All Nebadon watched in wonder.
124.b26.p: On March 20 he graduated from the synagogue school and was declared a “⟦Q 124:5.4|123:5.2⟧son of the commandment.⟦/Q⟧” His teachers and the elders planned to send him to the academy in Jerusalem, but Jesus grew more and more sure that he would not go. He did not yet know that he would soon lose his father and become the eldest brother and teacher of a large family.
124.b28.p: In April of A.D. 7, Jesus set out with his parents in a company of 103 on his first Passover pilgrimage. Because the Jews avoided dealing with Samaritans, they took the road down the Jordan valley. All along the way his parents told him old stories from the history of Israel.
124.b29.t: Past Shunem, Jezreel, and Mount Gilboa; camp by a spring in the Jordan valley
Past the Jabbok; camp at the foot of Mount Sartaba
Past Herod’s new villages; overnight at Jericho
Up the Mount of Olives and through Bethany to Jerusalem
124.b30.p: In Bethany the family stopped at the home of Simon, whose children were Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, and a lifelong friendship began. Never was Jesus gripped by such a purely human thrill as when he first looked on the holy city from the brow of Olivet. In the temple he was lost in thought and asked fewer questions, but he did ask why his Father in heaven required the slaughter of so many innocent animals.
124.b31.p: On the day before the Passover Sabbath, flood tides of spiritual illumination swept through his mind, and his heart overflowed with pity for the spiritually blind multitudes. That night, for the first time, a messenger sent by Immanuel appeared to him and told him that the time had come to begin his Father’s business. This was the first act in the long journey by which he would once again take upon his shoulders the responsibility of a universe.
124.b32.q: ⟦Q 124:6.18⟧Thus ends the career of the Nazareth lad, and begins the narrative of that adolescent youth—the increasingly self-conscious divine human⟦/Q⟧
124.b34.p: The Jesus of Paper 124 is a boy who already has a mind of his own. He questioned the law against pictures, admired the games of a Greek city, and asked whether the doorpost parchment was consistent with the rest of the law. Yet he always respected his parents’ decisions. He did not throw away either loyalty to his convictions or honor to his parents; he wove the two together into a solidarity of love. His mother’s illness laid the burden of the eldest son on him early, and he led his friends without ever fighting for his own rights. Growing up this way, the boy heard in Jerusalem the first call to begin his Father’s business. His mission ripened quietly in a time of ordinary growth and obedience.
124.b35.t: He spoke his mind but abided by his father’s decision
He first sensed his mission, and he did not fight for his own rights
His last year of play; the duties of the eldest son began
He reconciled loyalty to conviction and honor to parents through love
He became sure of his earth mission and became a son of the commandment
At his first Passover he heard the call to begin his Father’s business
124.b37.box: The boy Jesus learned to be true to his convictions while honoring his parents, and in that ordinary obedience he heard the call to begin his Father’s business.
125.title: Jesus at Jerusalem
125.b0.ask: “What disappointed the twelve-year-old Jesus when he first saw the temple at Jerusalem, and what did he resolve?”
125.b2.p: In the previous paper we saw the later childhood of the boy Jesus as he grew, learned, and worked in Nazareth. Now Paper 125 follows the first visit to Jerusalem that he could remember. No event in all his earth life was more fascinating or more humanly thrilling, and the days of the week after the Passover were his first taste of complete freedom from responsibility.
125.b3.p: Women were not required to go up to the Passover, but Jesus said he would not go unless his mother went too. Yet as soon as he passed through the temple gates, his disillusionment began. His mother had to go off to the women’s gallery, the ceremony of consecration was a mere formality, and the explanations of the rituals spoke of the wrath of God. The boy told Joseph that the heavenly Father could not love his children less than his earthly father loved him — and his parents never again tried to change his mind.
125.b4.p: What, then, troubled this twelve-year-old in the temple? What did he ask the teachers over four days? And with what resolve did he go home?
125.b5.q: “⟦Q 125:0.6⟧The heavenly Father cannot love his children less than you love me.⟦/Q⟧”
125.b8.p: Jesus was shocked by the spirit of irreverence he saw in the temple courts. In the court of the gentiles the money-changers and the sellers of sacrificial animals, the shouting and cursing, and the bleating of sheep were all mixed together, and painted courtesans walked about openly. He admired the feeling and ceremony of the temple, but in the faces of thoughtless worshipers he saw spiritual ugliness.
125.b9.p: In the court of the priests, the slaughter of droves of animals and the washing away of their blood were more than this nature-loving boy could bear. He clutched his father’s arm and begged to be taken away. Joseph wisely led him to the Gate Beautiful and explained the feasts at which Galileans attended temple worship three times a year.
125.b10.t: Seven weeks after the Passover — instituted by Moses
The feast of dedication and Purim
125.b12.p: Five families from Nazareth kept the Passover at the home of Simon in Bethany. As a new son of the covenant, Jesus was asked to tell the origin of the Passover. He did it well, yet he quietly worked in his impressions of what he had lately seen and heard, which embarrassed his parents. He was sure that his heavenly Father took no pleasure in the sight of sacrifices, and he became more and more determined someday to establish a bloodless celebration of the Passover.
125.b13.p: That night the boy hardly slept, troubled by dreams of slaughter. For the rest of the week he went about Jerusalem with Lazarus and spent most of his time at the teaching conferences near the temple. After a night spent in Bethany, Lazarus, Martha, and Mary came to love him like a brother. He also talked with more than one hundred and fifty boys of his age, learned how people lived in faraway lands, and began to long to travel all over the world.
125.b14.p: Several times his parents found their son alone, his head in his hands, deep in thought, and they did not know what to do. Before they left, they arranged for Jesus to come back at fifteen to study at the most famous rabbinical academy, but Jesus seemed indifferent.
125.b16.p: On the first day of the week after the Passover, the Nazareth company set out, the men and the women traveling in separate groups, as was the custom. Jesus was so absorbed in a temple discussion about angels that he did not notice the time to leave had passed. Each parent supposed he was with the other, and they did not discover he was missing until they reached Jericho.
125.b17.t: That Jesus was traveling with the men
That since Jesus had come up with the women, he was going back with them
Absorbed in the temple discussion, he realized it only at the noon recess
125.b18.h: 4. First and Second Days in the Temple
125.b19.p: On the first day Jesus only listened to the discussions in the quieted temple. Then he went back to Bethany and meditated alone in the garden. The next morning, from the brow of Olivet, he looked out over a people spiritually poor, bound by tradition, and watched over by Roman legions — and he wept.
125.b20.p: On the second day he joined boldly in the discussions with questions of his own, but always in a manner fitting his age. He asked whether it was just to put to death a drunken gentile who had wandered by mistake into the forbidden area. A narrow-minded teacher questioned his age and sneered that he was from Nazareth. But the leader insisted that the boy was not to blame, and Jesus was allowed to stay on as a student in the discussions.
125.b21.h: 5. The Third Day in the Temple
125.b22.p: On the third day a large crowd gathered, drawn by reports of a boy who was confounding the wise men of the law. Joseph and Mary went into the temple several times, but it never occurred to them to look among the discussion groups. Before the day was over, the attention of all the main groups had turned to Jesus’ questions.
125.b23.t: What really lies behind the veil?
Why must the mothers in Israel be separated from the men who worship?
If God is a loving father, why must so many animals be slaughtered?
Should barter and trade be allowed in the house of worship?
A prince on David’s throne, or the light of life in a spiritual kingdom?
125.b24.p: For more than four hours he taught by asking questions. He blended wisdom with humor, he was always fair, and he never took unfair advantage of anyone. He was free of any wish to win an argument for the sake of logical triumph. He cared only to proclaim truth and so reveal God more fully.
125.b25.q: ⟦Q 125:5.8⟧He conveyed his teaching by the questions he would ask.⟦/Q⟧
125.b26.p: That night he stayed late in the garden at Bethany, wrestling with how he might reveal a more beautiful idea of the heavenly Father to his spiritually blind countrymen and set them free from the bondage of tradition. But no clear light came.
125.b27.h: 6. The Fourth Day in the Temple
125.b28.p: On the afternoon of the fourth day, the leader seated the boy beside him and asked him to give his views on prayer and worship. Just then his parents, passing through the temple court, recognized their son’s voice. Mary scolded him in front of everyone, and her rebuke brought one of the greatest opportunities of his young life to an awkward end.
125.b29.p: After a moment’s thought, Jesus answered: since it was time for him to be about his Father’s business, should they not have expected to find him in his Father’s house? Then, when only his parents were left, he eased their distress by saying that no one had done anything but what he thought best. On the brow of Olivet he cried out, trembling, that he would return to cleanse the temple and deliver his people from their bondage.
125.b30.q: “⟦Q 125:6.11⟧While I must do the will of my Father in heaven, I will also be obedient to my father on earth. I will await my hour.⟦/Q⟧”
125.b31.p: He tried to conform even when he could not agree, and he was an artist at fitting his devotion to duty to the obligations of family loyalty and social service. Mary, for her part, took his words on Olivet as a prophecy of a Messianic mission as Israel’s deliverer, and she began to try to steer her son’s thinking in patriotic and nationalistic directions.
125.b33.p: Paper 125 shows the disillusionment and the resolve of a boy facing the realities of religion for the first time. Jesus was deeply troubled by the trading and the blood sacrifices in the temple and by the separation his mother had to endure. Yet he did not try to win by criticizing; he taught by asking questions. At the root of all his questions lay one conviction: the heavenly Father could not love less than an earthly father. And though he burned with longing for his mission, he chose to go home, obey his earthly father, and wait for his hour.
125.b34.t: The trading and blood sacrifices of the temple deeply shocked the boy
He was sure the heavenly Father takes no pleasure in sacrifices
Each parent thought he was with the other, and they left without him
First and Second Days in the Temple
He wept over his people and asked bold questions fitting his age
The Third Day in the Temple
With five questions he taught fairly, seeking only the truth
The Fourth Day in the Temple
He would do the Father’s will, obey his earthly father, and await his hour
125.b36.box: Sure of a loving Father, the boy chose to carry his longing for his mission in obedience, and to wait for his hour.
126.title: The Two Crucial Years
126.b0.ask: “How did a fourteen-year-old who had lost his father carry both the burden of his family and the question of his mission?”
126.b2.p: In Paper 125 Jesus came home to Nazareth from the temple in Jerusalem, burning with the awareness that he must begin his “Father’s business.” Paper 126 covers what followed: his fourteenth and fifteenth years, the most crucial and difficult two years of his earth life. He had begun to be self-conscious of his divinity and destiny, but he had not yet achieved much communication with his Thought Adjuster. These years were therefore a great test and a real trial.
126.b3.p: His parents did not understand their son, but they truly loved him. Jesus respected the sincere Pharisee and the honest scribe, but he despised hypocritical religious leaders. He was tempted to become the Messiah the Jews expected, yet he did not give in. The people of Nazareth expected him to become a great teacher in Israel.
126.b4.p: But just when the outlook seemed brightest, his father Joseph died. With all his plans in ruins, what did the boy hold on to? And how did he shape his sense of mission?
126.b5.q: ⟦Q 126:5.4⟧Jesus' life is the everlasting comfort of all disappointed idealists.⟦/Q⟧
126.b8.p: At fourteen Jesus made good yokes, worked skillfully with canvas and leather, and was fast becoming a carpenter and cabinetmaker. In summer he often climbed the hill northwest of Nazareth to pray and meditate, and he grew more and more aware of the nature of his bestowal. From there he looked out on Megiddo, Taanach, Dothan, Ebal and Gerizim, and he recalled the history and traditions of his father Joseph’s people.
126.b9.p: Joseph had put money aside so that Jesus could begin a long course of study in Jerusalem at fifteen. But his parents often doubted their son’s destiny. Dozens of times his mother waited for him to work a miracle, but nothing extraordinary ever happened. In those days people believed that a man of promise would prove his calling by wonders. Still, through this year it could truly be said that Jesus “⟦Q 126:1.7⟧grew in favor with man and with God,⟦/Q⟧” and the family’s future looked bright.
126.b11.p: On September 25, while working on the governor’s residence at Sepphoris, Joseph was badly hurt when a derrick fell, and he died before Mary could reach him. The carpenter boy, just past fourteen, now took on, along with his heavenly Father’s mission, the care of his widowed mother, seven brothers and sisters, and one more child yet unborn. The paper explains that this heavy but highly educational responsibility was permitted.
126.b12.p: Jesus accepted this responsibility willingly and carried it out faithfully to the end. He would not now study under the rabbis in Jerusalem, and he never received from any human source his authority to teach truth. He measured every institution and custom by the same test, and he devoted his life to two purposes: caring for his family and preparing to do his Father’s will. He was generous yet frugal, saving yet liberal.
126.b13.t: What does it do for the human soul?
The good an institution or custom does for the soul
Does it bring God to man?
Does it bring man to God?
Whether it leads people to God
126.b15.p: This year Jesus took firm charge of the family’s affairs, but their savings were nearly gone. In April the youngest child, Ruth, was born, and for almost twenty years Jesus cared for her more tenderly than anyone. He tried to teach the younger children to pray in their own words, and when this did not go as he hoped, one October evening he wrote out a standard family prayer in charcoal on a smooth cedar board. This was the first form of the prayer later known as “⟦Q 126:3.3⟧the Lord’s Prayer.⟦/Q⟧”
126.b16.p: He rightly reasoned that supporting his family was his first duty. And after thoroughly studying the Jewish ideas about the Messiah, he became sure that he was not that Messiah and would never sit on David’s throne. Reading “⟦Q 126:3.8|136:1.6⟧The Book of Enoch⟦/Q⟧” in the synagogue library, he was deeply moved by the term “⟦Q 126:3.6|126:3.8|0:5.3⟧Son of Man,⟦/Q⟧” and he decided then and there to take it as his title when he began his work.
126.b17.t: He would never sit on it
Never to be expected of him
A teacher for the Jews alone
The “⟦Q 126:3.6|126:3.8|0:5.3⟧Son of Man⟦/Q⟧” in the Book of Enoch
Nearest the truth — adopted as his title
126.b18.q: ⟦Q 126:3.8⟧Jesus had an unerring ability for the recognition of truth, and truth he never hesitated to embrace, no matter from what source it appeared to emanate⟦/Q⟧
126.b19.p: Yet confusion remained. Was he a Jew? Was he of the house of David? Could his mother be right? What should be his relation to his family, to the Jewish religion, to Rome, and to the gentiles? He turned these questions over as he worked at the carpenter’s bench. Little by little he learned not to reveal all his thoughts, and though he longed for a friend who would understand him, he carried his burdens alone.
126.b21.p: On the first Sabbath after his fifteenth birthday, Jesus conducted the morning service of the synagogue for the first time. He read passages of Scripture that he had chosen himself. The villagers had never seen him so solemn, so earnest, so manly and authoritative.
126.b22.t: “⟦Q 126:4.2|123:5.11⟧The spirit of the Lord God is upon me⟦/Q⟧”
To bind up the brokenhearted and proclaim liberty to the captives
Hate evil, love good, and establish judgment
Relieve the oppressed; defend the fatherless and the widow
“⟦Q 126:4.5⟧Wherewith shall I come before the Lord?⟦/Q⟧”
Not offerings, but to deal justly, love mercy, and walk humbly
“⟦Q 126:4.6⟧To whom, then, will you liken God?⟦/Q⟧”
He gives power to the weak; fear not
“⟦Q 126:4.7⟧You are my witness, says the Lord⟦/Q⟧”
Beside me there is no savior
126.b23.p: That afternoon he climbed the hill with James. When they came back, he wrote out the Ten Commandments in Greek on two boards. Martha painted them, and for a long time they hung on the wall above James’s workbench.
126.b25.p: The family slipped back more and more into simple living, and a carpenter’s wages fell to about twenty-five cents a day. When the tax collector threatened to take his harp, Jesus gave his copy of the Greek scriptures to the synagogue library as his coming-of-age offering. The hardest blow came at Sepphoris, when Herod ruled that nothing was owed to Joseph. After this unjust decision Jesus never again trusted Herod Antipas.
126.b26.p: All his plans seemed thwarted, yet he did not falter or lose heart. Day by day he faithfully met the duties in front of him. The hard experience of supporting his family protected him from drifting into idle meditation or mysticism. He rented land and gave each of his brothers and sisters a garden plot, adapting himself to reality and doing his best to meet his family’s hopes. With the end of his fifteenth year, his growth in body and mind came to a close, and the real career of this young man of Nazareth began.
126.b27.t: He worked from early morning till late at night
He gave his copy of the scriptures to the synagogue
He gave up the dream of a country farm and adapted to reality
He sent James to gather news of the world
126.b29.p: Paper 126 shows how a young man passed through the two hardest years of his life. His father’s death closed the road to study in Jerusalem and placed the family’s living on his shoulders, but Jesus accepted that burden willingly and faithfully met each day’s duties. At the same time, beside his workbench, he thought deeply about his mission, turned away from the path of a political Messiah, and chose the name “⟦Q 126:3.6|126:3.8|0:5.3⟧Son of Man.⟦/Q⟧” With no one to understand him, he carried his burdens alone — yet he did not waver. That is why his life is a comfort to every disappointed idealist.
126.b30.t: Praying on the hill, he grew more aware of the nature of his bestowal
At fourteen he became head of the family and willingly shouldered the load
He put aside the Messianic ideas and chose “⟦Q 126:3.6|126:3.8|0:5.3⟧Son of Man⟦/Q⟧”
He led his first service with scriptures of justice, mercy, and liberty
Even when thwarted he did not lose heart, but did each day’s duty
126.b32.box: Even with all his plans in ruins, Jesus faithfully did each day’s duty and so prepared for his mission.
127.title: The Adolescent Years
127.b0.ask: “From fifteen to twenty, how did the young head of a family grow, through trial after trial, into a full-grown man?”
127.b2.p: In Paper 126 Jesus lost his father and, at fifteen, became the head of a large family. Paper 127 follows his adolescent years from sixteen to twenty. Within a few years of his father’s death all the family property was gone, and Jesus came more and more fully to understand his prehuman existence and his purpose of revealing the Paradise Father.
127.b3.p: The paper says that no young person will ever be called to pass through harder tests than Jesus endured in those years from fifteen to twenty. Because he truly lived through adolescence, the Son of Man became a refuge that understands the troubled and perplexed young people of all worlds. Slowly but surely, through real experience, he was earning the right to be the sovereign of his universe.
127.b4.p: What, then, did this young man choose in the face of poverty, the turmoil of nationalism, a death in the family, and the love of a woman? And how did he become a man?
127.b5.q: ⟦Q 127:6.12⟧He is slowly learning how to live the heavenly life while he continues on with the earthly existence.⟦/Q⟧
127.b8.p: This year Jesus reached his full physical growth. He was calm and serious, yet kind and sympathetic, and even in the most ordinary meetings his twofold nature, human and divine, showed through. He always displayed the combination of a sympathetic friend and an authoritative teacher.
127.b9.p: His mother had told the family that Jesus was to be the deliverer of the Jewish people, so they were confused when he frankly denied such ideas. When the synagogue school would not take girls, Jesus ran a home school, holding that girls should learn just as boys did. By the end of the year he had nearly decided to raise his family and see his brothers and sisters married before beginning any public work. His mission was so unusual that no one could advise him about it, and so he spoke of it less and less.
127.b11.p: Opposition to paying taxes to Rome stirred up unrest, and a nationalist party arose that would soon be called the Zealots. Jesus listened carefully to its organizers and asked many questions, but he refused to join. His mother, his uncle, and even his brother James urged him to enlist, and Isaac, a wealthy moneylender, offered to support the family if he would become a leader.
127.b12.p: Unable to reveal that he was more than a man, he turned for the first time to a conscious public strategy. Bravely and diplomatically, he explained that his first duty was to his family — that his widowed mother and his eight brothers and sisters needed a father’s care and guidance. A speech by James helped him through the crisis, but the division of feeling in Nazareth never healed. This became one of the chief reasons for the later move to Capernaum.
127.b14.t: Not waiting for a Messiah, but turning to political revolt
They urged him to join the nationalist cause
He offered to support the family if Jesus would lead
The only wise counselor in Nazareth
He declined, pointing to his duty to his family
127.b15.p: During this year, by the power of his own decisions and the help of his indwelling Monitor alone, he steadily brought together his divine and human natures.
127.b17.p: Everything the family owned was sold except the house and the garden. Jesus took James up to the Passover and told him the history of the places along the way, just as their father had once done for him. In the temple discussions he asked no questions at all, and to the disappointed James he said only, “⟦Q 127:3.5|100:7.14|128:1.15⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
127.b18.p: Back home he worked in the old repair shop near the caravan lot and greatly enjoyed meeting ordinary people from all over the country. In September Elizabeth and John came to visit, and the two young men agreed not to meet again until the heavenly Father called them. In December the youngest, Amos, died of a high fever, and Mary at last accepted Jesus as the true head of the family.
127.b19.p: When poverty deepened and funeral costs were added, Jesus encouraged his mother: grief did not help, but her smile could inspire the children. His steady, practical optimism was contagious, and the children looked forward to better days and grew in noble character. He could live “⟦Q 102:2.8⟧as seeing Him who is invisible.⟦/Q⟧”
127.b21.p: Jesus persuaded his mother to give up the old way of forbidding evil and instead to teach the children with positive commands to do good. All his life he gave counsel in the form “⟦Q 127:4.2⟧you shall do this,⟦/Q⟧” and he never stressed evil by forbidding it. Punishment was hardly ever needed. On the rare occasions when Jude was punished, it was only with the unanimous agreement of the older children and Jude’s own consent. His fairness and personal consideration won the love of the whole family.
127.b22.t: Character as the paper draws it
A faithful worker who kept steadily at it
A well-meaning boy, but too much of a dreamer
High ideals, but an unstable temperament
Keen of spiritual insight, and calm
The sunshine of the home, with the truest heart
127.b23.p: He liberalized the family’s customs, including the keeping of the Sabbath, and Mary agreed wholeheartedly. To pay for Jude’s schooling, he even sold his beloved harp.
127.b25.p: Poor as he was, Jesus was one of the finest young men in Nazareth, and Rebecca, the eldest daughter of Ezra, a wealthy merchant, fell in love with him. Mary and Miriam tried to discourage her, but this only strengthened her resolve, and with her father’s help she invited Jesus to her seventeenth birthday party.
127.b26.p: Jesus kindly explained that no amount of money could take the place of his personal duty to raise his father’s family. Sincerely grateful for Rebecca’s admiration, he told her that he could not think of marriage until he had fulfilled his first duty to his family, and that he should not take on lifelong obligations before his destiny had been made clear. The paper says that he was truly “⟦Q 119:6.6|128:1.5⟧in all points tested.⟦/Q⟧” Rebecca moved away to Sepphoris, but she waited for him all her life. During the years of his public work she followed him devotedly, and she stood beside the cross.
127.b28.p: From this time on, people’s affection for him took on the quality of worshipful, admiring respect. Jesus kept the Passover at Bethany with Lazarus, Martha, and Mary — without the paschal lamb. He shared unleavened bread and wine, calling them “⟦Q 127:6.7|121:5.12|130:8.3⟧the bread of life⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 127:6.7|34:6.8|143:5.10⟧the water of life,⟦/Q⟧” and afterward he celebrated this sacrament every time he visited Bethany. At home, however, he went on keeping the Passover with his family “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧according to the law of Moses.⟦/Q⟧”
127.b29.p: When his mother asked him about marriage, he answered that everything must wait for “my hour.” At twenty, Jesus was fast becoming a grown man. The paper lists, one by one, what he learned in these years.
127.b30.t: He learned well how to bear it
He kept on bravely when his plans were thwarted
He stayed fair and just even in the face of injustice
He adjusted spiritual ideals to the practical demands of earthly life
He worked toward the near need and the distant ideal together
He lived the heavenly life within the earthly one
He turned the difficulties of time into the triumphs of eternity
127.b31.q: ⟦Q 127:6.13⟧He is our understanding brother, sympathetic friend, experienced sovereign, and merciful father.⟦/Q⟧
127.b32.p: Having put in order in his youth the knowledge he gathered as a child, he now stood on the threshold of full manhood, filled with sympathy for the weaknesses of human nature. He was ready to carry on his supreme mission: to reveal God to man and to lead man to God.
127.b34.p: Paper 127 shows us not grand miracles but the heavy days of an ordinary young man. Jesus turned down the fervor of nationalism and a generous offer of support. He bore the death of his youngest brother and deepening poverty. He even declined, with courtesy, the sincere love of a young woman, for the sake of his duty to his family. He passed through all these trials with practical optimism and positive teaching, learning to fit ideals to reality and to turn the difficulties of time into the triumphs of eternity. Because he lived his adolescence to the full, he became a brother who understands every troubled young person.
127.b35.t: Fully grown in body, he began to carry his mission alone
He refused the nationalist movement and chose his duty to his family
Even after losing his youngest brother, he lifted the family with practical optimism
He raised the children with positive commands, not prohibitions
For duty and destiny he gently declined a sincere love
He became a man who had learned to live the heavenly life on earth
127.b37.box: Having lived to the full an adolescence filled with trials, Jesus became a brother who understands every young person, and an experienced sovereign.
